cards.title: The Rule of Law
cards.hook: The principle that everyone — including those in power — is bound by the same publicly known laws, applied equally.

cards.title: What Government Is For
cards.hook: Every society needs a way to make and enforce collective decisions — that shared system of authority is what we call government.

cards.title: The Declaration of Independence
cards.hook: It's remembered for 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness' — but most of the Declaration is a long list of grievances: a case that a government had broken faith with the governed.

cards.title: When a Precedent Loses Its Foundation
cards.hook: A 1980 ruling barred the Ten Commandments from public classrooms. An appeals court says the test it rested on is gone — so the ruling is too. That claim is now at the Supreme Court.

cards.title: The Federalist Papers
cards.hook: To sell a skeptical public on the new Constitution, three founders wrote 85 newspaper essays under a single fake name. They're still the best guide to what it means.

cards.title: Political Legitimacy
cards.hook: Power can rest on fear alone, but it lasts when people believe it is rightful. That belief — legitimacy — is what separates authority from mere force.

cards.title: The Social Contract
cards.hook: Why should anyone obey the state? The social contract answers: people trade some freedom for the security and order that only collective authority can provide.

cards.title: Separation of Powers
cards.hook: Split government into branches that make, enforce, and interpret the law — so no single part can do all three.

cards.title: Air Force One and the Modern Presidency
cards.hook: A historian's argument that the presidency we recognize today — constantly travelling, personally diplomatic, permanently campaigning — was built by an airplane.

cards.title: Who Actually Sets the Rules for a Federal Election
cards.hook: The Constitution hands the times, places and manner of congressional elections to state legislatures, with Congress able to override. The president is not on that list.

cards.title: Can the President Fire the Heads of Independent Agencies?
cards.hook: For 91 years, a 1935 precedent shielded independent agency heads from being fired at a president's will. In 2026 the Supreme Court swept most of that shield away.

cards.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
cards.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

cards.title: Who Decides What to Charge
cards.hook: A prosecutor builds a case; headquarters picks the charge. That chain of command is normal — and it is also the point where a case can be quietly downgraded.

cards.title: Who Gets to Set the Size of the Court
cards.hook: Nine justices feels constitutional. It is not — the number is ordinary law, which is exactly why proposals to freeze it at nine keep appearing.

cards.title: How Much Deference Does the Military Get?
cards.hook: Courts scrutinize government classifications closely — except in the military, where judges have long deferred. A transgender service ban now tests where that deference stops.

cards.title: The Supreme Court of Israel
cards.hook: A court that built constitutional review out of ordinary statutes, opened its doors to almost any petitioner — and is now, for the first time, itself the central issue in a national election.

cards.title: A Right With No Way to Sue Is Half a Right
cards.hook: A prisoner's religious rights were violated and the harm was already done. The hard legal question was not whether it was wrong — it was whether he could recover anything at all.

cards.title: You Can Donate to the Government — You Can't Direct It
cards.hook: Private money paying for a public building sounds like a bargain for taxpayers. Under U.S. law it mostly isn't allowed, because the power to decide what government spends belongs to Congress.

cards.title: When Federal Law Means Different Things in Different States
cards.hook: Nine federal appeals courts have read the same detention statute; seven say one thing and two say the opposite. Until the Supreme Court steps in, your rights depend on your address.

cards.title: How Far Does One Judge's Order Reach?
cards.hook: A court can block a policy for the people who sued — or for everyone, everywhere. The scope of an injunction can matter as much as who won.

cards.title: Losing in Court Isn't Always the End of a Policy
cards.hook: A court judgment binds the order in front of it. Rewrite the order and the clock restarts at the bottom of the judicial ladder — sometimes for years.

cards.title: The Presumption of Regularity
cards.hook: Courts normally start by assuming the government followed its own rules and told the truth. That default is quiet, load-bearing — and, judges are now saying out loud, forfeitable.

cards.title: Firing an Official Can Require a Hearing First
cards.hook: The fight over removing a Federal Reserve governor turned on something narrower than presidential power: whether she gets told the charge and a chance to answer before she is out.

cards.title: The Supreme Court of Japan
cards.hook: Japan's top court has the power of constitutional review and almost never uses it: roughly ten laws struck down in eighty years, against 900-plus in the United States.

cards.title: Strings Attached: When Federal Money Becomes Leverage
cards.hook: A national government that can't order regions around directly can often get the same result by attaching conditions to its money — which is why courts ask where persuasion ends and coercion begins.

cards.title: The Pardon Isn't for Sale. The Advocacy Is.
cards.hook: Paying for a presidential pardon outright would be a crime. Paying someone up to $5 million to get you in front of the president to ask for one? Perfectly legal — and a growing D.C. industry.

cards.title: The 60-Day Clock That Keeps Getting Reset
cards.hook: The War Powers Resolution gives Congress 60 days to approve a war before the president must stop — but a new 'notice' can restart the clock, and Congress has struggled to make its objection stick.

cards.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
cards.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

cards.title: When Congress Overrides the Court
cards.hook: A high court's ruling isn't always the last word. When judges interpret a statute, the legislature can often just rewrite the law — unless the decision rests on the constitution itself.

cards.title: Checks and Balances
cards.hook: Separating power isn't enough — each branch also gets tools to limit the others, so power keeps power in check.

cards.title: The Executive
cards.hook: Laws don't enforce themselves. The executive is the branch that runs the state day to day — carrying out the law, commanding the bureaucracy, and acting in a crisis.

cards.title: The Legislature
cards.hook: The branch that makes the law is also where a society argues out loud — the legislature turns competing interests into binding rules through debate and votes.

cards.title: Why an Agency Is Harder to Abolish Than to Announce
cards.hook: A president can reshape an agency's leadership and priorities quickly. Erasing it is a different act, because the agency exists in statute and its money is appropriated by Congress.

cards.title: Censure: Punishment Without Removal
cards.hook: Legislatures mostly cannot fire their own members easily — voters hired them. So they built a middle sanction: a formal, recorded statement that the chamber disapproves.

cards.title: When Supreme Court Justices Rode the Circuit
cards.hook: For over a century, sitting on the Supreme Court meant months on horseback hearing ordinary cases. Some reformers want a version of that back — and the reasons are revealing.

cards.title: The Supreme Court's Other Docket
cards.hook: The Court hears about sixty argued cases a year and disposes of thousands more by short written order. Most of what it does never gets an opinion at all.

cards.title: The Appeal After the Last Appeal
cards.hook: When the Supreme Court declines your case, one option remains: ask it to reconsider. It has not granted such a request since 2018.

cards.title: What a Chief Justice Actually Controls
cards.hook: The chief justice's vote counts the same as everyone else's. The real power is procedural — who speaks, who writes, and in what order — and none of it is in the Constitution.

cards.title: Reading a Justice by the Numbers
cards.hook: Label a judge 'conservative' and you've explained almost nothing. Code 311 of Barrett's decisions and a sharper pattern appears: she asks whether a ruling reaches further than the authority behind it.

cards.title: Who Are the "Friends of the Court"?
cards.hook: Most briefs a supreme court reads are filed by people who aren't suing anyone. The amicus brief is how outside interests get a say in a case they are not party to.

cards.title: Beyond the Swing Justice
cards.hook: The 'swing vote' is a lazy model of a nine-member court. Sort four terms of close cases and you get two distinct jobs: building narrow majorities, and bridging the dissents nobody won.

cards.title: How Many Jurors Make a Jury?
cards.hook: Everyone pictures twelve. But in 1970 the Supreme Court called that number a 'historical accident' — and now it has agreed to look again.

cards.title: A Law 'Trapped in Amber'
cards.hook: One throwaway metaphor from a Supreme Court opinion is now everywhere in the lower courts — and scholars disagree about whether it smuggles in a whole theory of the constitution.

cards.title: What a Concurrence Is For
cards.hook: A concurring justice agrees with the outcome — and sometimes uses the space to propose demolishing the doctrine the majority just applied. Today's lone concurrence is tomorrow's majority.

cards.title: Can You Predict a Ruling from Oral Argument?
cards.hook: Courtroom folk wisdom says the side that gets grilled hardest is the side that loses. Someone finally checked the numbers — and the rule works, but barely better than a coin flip.

cards.title: Nine Justices, Nine Styles
cards.hook: One scholar coded 5,095 questions from a full Supreme Court term and found each justice interrogates lawyers in a signature way — a fingerprint of how they think about the law.

cards.title: Supreme Court Term Limits
cards.hook: U.S. Supreme Court justices serve for life — unusual among democracies. A recurring reform would swap that for fixed terms. Why the idea keeps returning, and why it's so hard to enact.

cards.title: Do People Trust the Court, or Just Their Side of It?
cards.hook: Only 46% of Americans approve of the Supreme Court overall — but break it down by party, and the real story is a 56-point gap in how Republicans and Democrats see the same institution.

cards.title: The Law That Keeps Living Faces Off Money
cards.hook: A new $1 coin puts a sitting president's face on U.S. currency for only the second time ever. Legal experts say the law was written to prevent exactly that.

cards.title: Why Texas Dominates the Supreme Court's Docket
cards.hook: Of the 35 cases with individual litigants the Supreme Court heard this term, five centered on Texans — more than double any other state. It's not Texas law that's unusual; it's the plumbing above it.

cards.title: Congress Holds the Court's Purse Strings, Too
cards.hook: The judiciary doesn't get to set its own budget. In July 2026, Justices Kagan and Barrett had to go to Capitol Hill and ask for one — like any other federal agency.

cards.title: There's No 25th Amendment for Congress
cards.hook: When a president is incapacitated, the Constitution has a formal fix: the 25th Amendment. When a senator is hospitalized for weeks with no details given, there isn't one.

cards.title: Why No Cameras in the Supreme Court?
cards.hook: You can read every Supreme Court ruling, but you can't watch the arguments on video. The long fight over courtroom cameras is really a fight over judicial transparency.

cards.title: How Precedent Erodes
cards.hook: Courts rarely kill an old ruling outright. More often it dies slowly — narrowed, distinguished, and ignored until little is left.

cards.title: The Power of a Dissent
cards.hook: A dissenting judge loses the case — but a sharp dissent can outlive the majority, persuading future courts or pushing lawmakers to rewrite the rule.

cards.title: The Senate Parliamentarian
cards.hook: The Senate's nonpartisan rules referee — an unelected adviser who can quietly reshape major bills by ruling on what the chamber's own procedures allow.

cards.title: The Director of National Intelligence
cards.hook: After 9/11, the U.S. created one job to make its spy agencies talk to each other — and a veteran argues the role needs expertise, not just political loyalty.

cards.title: When Judges Step Aside
cards.hook: A judge who might be biased is supposed to step aside. But on the U.S. Supreme Court, each justice decides that alone — and no one can overrule them.

cards.title: When Legal Tools Switch Sides
cards.hook: Doctrines aren't ideologies. Watch one Supreme Court term closely and you can see arguments long branded conservative being made by liberals, and vice versa.

cards.title: Where a 'Right to Privacy' Comes From
cards.hook: The word 'privacy' never appears in the U.S. Constitution. Decades of doctrine hang on where courts decided to find it — and a long-running argument says they looked in the wrong place.

cards.title: The Constitution Has Clauses Courts Won't Touch
cards.hook: Not every line in the Constitution gets fought over in court. Some, like the ban on quartering soldiers, have sat almost untouched for over two centuries — by choice, not by accident.

cards.title: What a Court Minority Can Actually Force
cards.hook: A losing bloc on a court can write a blistering dissent, or it can hold a procedural lever. Only one of those changes what the court does.

cards.title: The One-Justice Order That Freezes a Case
cards.hook: Before the Supreme Court decides anything, a single justice can push pause. That's how White House ballroom construction kept going after two lower courts had ordered it stopped.

cards.title: The 'Tenth Justice': Government's Lawyer at the Court
cards.hook: One lawyer appears in most Supreme Court cases, keeps an office inside the courthouse, and shapes what the Court decides by choosing which questions to put in front of it.

cards.title: What an Executive Order Can and Cannot Change
cards.hook: A presidential order can tell the executive branch what to aim for. It can't skip the process an agency must follow — which is why headlines and reality often diverge.

cards.title: The Memo Congress Never Voted On
cards.hook: A presidential memorandum can direct 200-plus FBI task forces to hunt down a whole ideology — no bill, no vote, and no requirement it even be made public.

cards.title: The Hearing Before the Job: How Senate Confirmation Works
cards.hook: Cabinet secretaries don't just get appointed — the Senate gets a vote first. A contentious July 2026 hearing for the next attorney general shows the confirmation gauntlet at work.

cards.title: The Supreme Court's 'Shadow Docket'
cards.hook: Most Supreme Court rulings today aren't fully-argued opinions — they're fast, often unsigned orders with little explanation. In the term ending October 2025, those quietly became the majority.

cards.title: Not All Dissents Are Created Equal
cards.hook: Dissent tallies treat a one-line 'I would deny' the same as a fully reasoned opinion. One scholar sorted 386 of them on the emergency docket — and found about half were just bare votes.

cards.title: A Law Can Take Effect Before Courts Decide If It's Legal
cards.hook: Texas requires parental permission before minors can download most apps. Courts haven't ruled it constitutional — but the Supreme Court's emergency docket let it take effect anyway.

cards.title: The Calendar as a Legal Strategy
cards.hook: Courts avoid changing election rules close to voting day. That gives a litigant a strange incentive: argue the other side sued too early, and the clock does the rest.

cards.title: What Federalism Is
cards.hook: Some countries split authority between a national government and regional ones, each with powers the other can't simply override.

cards.title: The Housing Policy That Sits Between a Shelter and a Home
cards.hook: Building apartments takes years. Emergency shelters help for a night. Tiny house villages spread because they fit the gap — and because local rules allow them faster.

cards.title: When Locking People Up Is the Local Jobs Plan
cards.hook: Rural places have sold prison beds to distant governments since the 1800s. Immigration detention has revived the trade — and with it an economy that grows only when enforcement does.

cards.title: Who Gets to Decide What Goes on a Map
cards.hook: Renaming a lake is not a matter of announcing it. In the U.S. a name normally climbs from town to county to state to a federal board — and stops entirely at the border.

cards.title: When the Law Carves Out an Exception for Belief
cards.hook: Idaho parents can decline medical care for a sick child on religious grounds and be shielded from prosecution. That exemption is not ancient — a federal funding rule helped create it.

cards.title: The Census Decides How Many Seats You Get
cards.hook: A once-a-decade headcount sets each state's share of the House for ten years. A Florida challenge argues the count was done wrong — and shows why that is nearly impossible to fix afterward.

cards.title: Strings Attached: When Federal Money Becomes Leverage
cards.hook: A national government that can't order regions around directly can often get the same result by attaching conditions to its money — which is why courts ask where persuasion ends and coercion begins.

cards.title: Mission Creep: When a Body Outgrows Its Stated Job
cards.hook: Memphis got a federal task force announced to fight violent crime. Ten months on, it had driven a surge of immigration arrests — mostly of people with no convictions. A study in how missions drift.

cards.title: Who Gets to Regulate Betting on Elections?
cards.hook: Wisconsin says you can't bet on an election you vote in — a law from 1849. The biggest prediction market calls that 'voter suppression.' Underneath sits a bigger question: which government decides?

cards.title: Abortion After Dobbs
cards.hook: In 2022 the Supreme Court did something rare: it withdrew a constitutional right it had recognized for half a century — and handed the question back to the states.

cards.title: When Federal Law Overrides the States
cards.hook: Who decides what warning goes on a bottle of weed killer — a state jury or the federal government? The answer turns on a quiet but powerful rule called preemption.

cards.title: Why an Agency Is Harder to Abolish Than to Announce
cards.hook: A president can reshape an agency's leadership and priorities quickly. Erasing it is a different act, because the agency exists in statute and its money is appropriated by Congress.

cards.title: Zoning as a Housing Policy Lever: the "Missing Middle"
cards.hook: Nearly 70% of Denver's residential land allows only single-family houses. A simulator estimates that letting four units build anywhere would raise market-rate multifamily supply 46%.

cards.title: Tribal Nations as a Third Sovereign
cards.hook: American federalism is usually taught as states versus Washington. That leaves out hundreds of tribal governments whose authority predates the Constitution itself.

cards.title: How a Federal Agency Changes Its Own Rules — No New Law Required
cards.hook: After a string of deadly shootings tied to its officers, ICE didn't wait for Congress to act. It just changed its own internal policy — a reminder of how much agencies can do on their own.

cards.title: States Are Writing AI Law First — and Federal Preemption Looms Over All of It
cards.hook: With no comprehensive federal AI law yet, states have become the testing ground for regulating artificial intelligence. That leaves every state AI law exposed to a preemption fight.

cards.title: Why It's So Hard to Sue Your Health Insurer
cards.hook: A 1974 law meant to protect pensions also quietly shields most employer health plans from lawsuits over wrongly denied claims — even when the denial causes real harm.

cards.title: Who Commands the National Guard?
cards.hook: The National Guard answers to two masters at once — a state governor and the president. A 2026 stand-off over troops in D.C. shows what happens when they pull in different directions.

cards.title: Who Decides Where the Data Center Goes?
cards.hook: A data center brings jobs and tax revenue — and noise, pollution, and higher power bills. Deciding whether to host one is a stress test for local democracy.

cards.title: Local Government
cards.hook: The layer of government you meet most often isn't the national one — it's the city or council that runs your streets, schools, and rubbish collection.

cards.title: Unitary vs Federal Systems
cards.hook: Where does the final say live — with one national government, or shared with regions? That choice shapes how a country is run.

cards.title: Tribal Water Rights & Interstate Compacts
cards.hook: Seven states share the Colorado River under a 100-year-old compact that barely mentions the tribes with some of the oldest legal claims to its water. Updating that deal is proving hard.

cards.title: Devolution & Confederation
cards.hook: Between a single central government and a loose alliance of states lies a spectrum — and where power sits on it shapes who can really decide.

cards.title: Who Actually Pays to Run an Election
cards.hook: National elections are run by local governments on local budgets. The people closest to the ballots are usually the ones worrying about affording them.

cards.title: When a Temporary Deployment Stops Being Temporary
cards.hook: Emergency powers rarely end with an announcement. They end — or don't — through quiet extensions that never get the scrutiny the first decision did.

cards.title: Local Officials Run the Election; Federal Money Defends It
cards.hook: Thousands of county and city offices actually run American elections — but the cyber defense behind them leans on federal money and expertise. When that support pauses, the vulnerability is local.

cards.title: When a Governor Pauses an Entire Industry by Executive Order
cards.hook: Data-center fights used to be decided lot by lot, in local zoning meetings. In 2026 a governor skipped that entirely and paused the whole industry statewide.

cards.title: Presidential vs Parliamentary
cards.hook: Two democracies can run on totally different wiring: in one, voters pick the leader directly; in the other, the legislature does — and that changes everything downstream.

cards.title: Democracy vs Authoritarianism
cards.hook: The deepest dividing line between regimes isn't left versus right — it's whether power can be lost. Can the people remove their rulers, or not?

cards.title: The Supreme Court of Israel
cards.hook: A court that built constitutional review out of ordinary statutes, opened its doors to almost any petitioner — and is now, for the first time, itself the central issue in a national election.

cards.title: How You Put a Number on Human Rights
cards.hook: Rights either exist or they don't — so how does anyone score a country? Researchers do it by reading the reports, coding the incidents, and correcting for a nasty bias.

cards.title: The Supreme Court of Japan
cards.hook: Japan's top court has the power of constitutional review and almost never uses it: roughly ten laws struck down in eighty years, against 900-plus in the United States.

cards.title: The Constitutional Court of South Africa
cards.hook: Born out of the end of apartheid, this court was designed to make a new constitution stick — and became one of the world's most-cited voices on what rights a government owes its people.

cards.title: The European Court of Justice
cards.hook: A court above nations: it doesn't replace any country's supreme court, but it makes sure EU law means the same thing in every member state.

cards.title: Electoral vs Liberal Democracy
cards.hook: Holding elections isn't the whole of democracy. Without rights, courts, and limits on the winner, voting alone can deliver an elected strongman.

cards.title: Supreme Court Term Limits
cards.hook: U.S. Supreme Court justices serve for life — unusual among democracies. A recurring reform would swap that for fixed terms. Why the idea keeps returning, and why it's so hard to enact.

cards.title: Monarchies, Republics & Regime Types
cards.hook: Is the head of state a queen or a president? That old question — monarchy or republic — turns out to matter less than whether real power is elected and accountable.

cards.title: Democratic Backsliding
cards.hook: Democracies rarely die in a single coup anymore. More often they erode — legally, gradually, step by step — until little is left but the shell of elections.

cards.title: The People With No Opinion
cards.hook: Researchers looking for antidemocratic attitudes kept finding something else: not opposition, not support, but a shrug. They argue the shrug is what makes erosion possible.

cards.title: Why Living Leaders Almost Never Appear on Money — Unless They're Royalty
cards.hook: A count of nearly 1,000 world coins found sitting leaders appear almost exclusively in hereditary monarchies — which is why putting an elected president on currency reads as a monarchical move.

cards.title: The Declaration of Independence
cards.hook: It's remembered for 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness' — but most of the Declaration is a long list of grievances: a case that a government had broken faith with the governed.

cards.title: The Ancient Origins of Politics
cards.hook: The words we still use — politics, democracy, republic — were coined in ancient Greece and Rome, where the first experiments in self-rule were run.

cards.title: The Founder Who Became a Verb
cards.hook: Elbridge Gerry signed the Declaration of Independence and served as vice president. He is remembered for a single map he signed in 1812 — and for the insult built from his name.

cards.title: How Out-of-Work Fishermen Aided the Revolution
cards.hook: When Britain choked off New England's fisheries, thousands of skilled sailors lost their livelihoods overnight — and Washington gained the experienced seamen he badly needed.

cards.title: Air Force One and the Modern Presidency
cards.hook: A historian's argument that the presidency we recognize today — constantly travelling, personally diplomatic, permanently campaigning — was built by an airplane.

cards.title: The Beating That Asked: Is Some Speech Itself Violence?
cards.hook: In 1856, a congressman beat a senator unconscious with a cane over an anti-slavery speech — and forced America to argue over whether words can be treated as an act of violence.

cards.title: A Pattern Two Centuries Old: Backing the Opposition, Denying It Officially
cards.hook: In 1805 a Venezuelan revolutionary asked Jefferson for help overthrowing Spanish rule. Jefferson denied involvement but quietly let him go — a pattern historians trace to 2026.

cards.title: The Federalist Papers
cards.hook: To sell a skeptical public on the new Constitution, three founders wrote 85 newspaper essays under a single fake name. They're still the best guide to what it means.

cards.title: The Enlightenment & Modern Politics
cards.hook: The radical idea that legitimate power comes from the people — not God or birth — was forged in the Enlightenment, and it still underpins democracy today.

cards.title: The History of Democracy
cards.hook: Democracy isn't a permanent gift — it's a hard-won, on-and-off achievement that nearly vanished for two thousand years before its modern comeback.

cards.title: When Supreme Court Justices Rode the Circuit
cards.hook: For over a century, sitting on the Supreme Court meant months on horseback hearing ordinary cases. Some reformers want a version of that back — and the reasons are revealing.

cards.title: A Law 'Trapped in Amber'
cards.hook: One throwaway metaphor from a Supreme Court opinion is now everywhere in the lower courts — and scholars disagree about whether it smuggles in a whole theory of the constitution.

cards.title: The Politics of Spectacle
cards.hook: Bread and circuses, military parades, staged combat — leaders have always used spectacle to project power and bind people to a shared identity.

cards.title: Key Political Thinkers
cards.hook: A handful of thinkers, writing across two millennia, still frame the questions we argue about: who should rule, why obey, and how to stop power going bad?

cards.title: Montesquieu's Other Warning: The Tyranny of Opinion
cards.hook: Montesquieu is famous for separation of powers. His lesser-known warning: a constitution can be free on paper and still fail, once enough people stop believing its limits apply to them.

cards.title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
cards.hook: An idea becomes binding law only after a journey: drafting, committee review, debate, votes, and final approval.

cards.title: Why a Handful of Members Can Stall a Whole Agenda
cards.hook: In a legislature with a thin majority, a bloc of a dozen members who vote together holds a veto — which is why intra-party factions often matter more than the other party does.

cards.title: The Stopgap: Governing by Deadline
cards.hook: Legislatures are supposed to pass budgets. When they cannot agree, many just extend last year's spending a few months at a time — and the deadline becomes the real negotiation.

cards.title: Who Gets to Set the Size of the Court
cards.hook: Nine justices feels constitutional. It is not — the number is ordinary law, which is exactly why proposals to freeze it at nine keep appearing.

cards.title: One Party, Both Chambers, Still No Bill
cards.hook: Republicans hold the White House and both chambers of Congress. A signature voting bill is stuck anyway — a case study in why controlling government isn't the same as controlling the Senate.

cards.title: A President Can Let a Bill Become Law by Doing Nothing
cards.hook: Signing isn't the only way a bill becomes law — sometimes doing nothing at all has the exact same effect.

cards.title: When Federal Law Overrides the States
cards.hook: Who decides what warning goes on a bottle of weed killer — a state jury or the federal government? The answer turns on a quiet but powerful rule called preemption.

cards.title: When Congress Overrides the Court
cards.hook: A high court's ruling isn't always the last word. When judges interpret a statute, the legislature can often just rewrite the law — unless the decision rests on the constitution itself.

cards.title: What a Constitution Is
cards.hook: The rulebook above the rules: a constitution sets out how a government is structured and the limits on its power.

cards.title: When DNA Evidence Outlasts the Statute of Limitations
cards.hook: A crime can go unprosecuted forever once its statute of limitations runs out — even if DNA later identifies a suspect. Massachusetts is one of the last states moving to close that gap.

cards.title: The Power of a Dissent
cards.hook: A dissenting judge loses the case — but a sharp dissent can outlive the majority, persuading future courts or pushing lawmakers to rewrite the rule.

cards.title: The Senate Parliamentarian
cards.hook: The Senate's nonpartisan rules referee — an unelected adviser who can quietly reshape major bills by ruling on what the chamber's own procedures allow.

cards.title: Statute Law vs Common Law
cards.hook: Not all law is written by legislators. Some of it is built up, case by case, by judges — and these two sources of law work very differently.

cards.title: Amending a Constitution
cards.hook: A constitution has to last — but not freeze. Amendment rules let it change deliberately, usually demanding more agreement than an ordinary law.

cards.title: How Precedent Erodes
cards.hook: Courts rarely kill an old ruling outright. More often it dies slowly — narrowed, distinguished, and ignored until little is left.

cards.title: What Democracy Means
cards.hook: Rule by the people: a system where political power ultimately traces back to citizens, usually through regular, free elections.

cards.title: Don't Trust the Name on the PAC
cards.hook: The cheapest way to disguise who is talking to voters isn't a lie in the ad — it's a reassuring name on the group paying for it.

cards.title: Who Can Vote: Suffrage
cards.hook: Democracy means rule by the people — but for most of history, 'the people' meant a narrow few. The story of suffrage is the slow widening of that circle.

cards.title: You Don't Have to Live in the District You Represent
cards.hook: The Constitution asks a House candidate to be an inhabitant of the state — not the district. That gap is why 'carpetbagger' is an insult and not a disqualification.

cards.title: The Founder Who Became a Verb
cards.hook: Elbridge Gerry signed the Declaration of Independence and served as vice president. He is remembered for a single map he signed in 1812 — and for the insult built from his name.

cards.title: Who Actually Pays to Run an Election
cards.hook: National elections are run by local governments on local budgets. The people closest to the ballots are usually the ones worrying about affording them.

cards.title: Who Actually Sets the Rules for a Federal Election
cards.hook: The Constitution hands the times, places and manner of congressional elections to state legislatures, with Congress able to override. The president is not on that list.

cards.title: A Voting Rule Needs a System Behind It
cards.hook: Writing a new election rule is the easy part. Building the machinery that can execute it before the next election is where rules quietly turn into disenfranchisement.

cards.title: Prices Vote: Economic Conditions and the Incumbent
cards.hook: Voters rarely audit a governing record line by line. They ask a cruder question — is life more affordable than it was? — and that question moves elections more reliably than most policy debates.

cards.title: How Official Statistics Earn Trust
cards.hook: A government statistic carries weight only because of the process behind it. When a report skips the usual methodology and review, the number stops being evidence and becomes an argument.

cards.title: Why Almost No Lawmakers Come From Working-Class Jobs
cards.hook: Working-class people are about half the US labor force and about 1% of its lawmakers. The bottleneck isn't voters — it's who ever gets to run.

cards.title: Why Noncitizen Voting Cases Are Hard to Prosecute
cards.hook: A rule can be clear and the enforcement still collapse. Charging noncitizens with voting means proving they knew they were ineligible — and that is where the cases fall apart.

cards.title: How Far Does One Judge's Order Reach?
cards.hook: A court can block a policy for the people who sued — or for everyone, everywhere. The scope of an injunction can matter as much as who won.

cards.title: The Calendar as a Legal Strategy
cards.hook: Courts avoid changing election rules close to voting day. That gives a litigant a strange incentive: argue the other side sued too early, and the clock does the rest.

cards.title: Dealignment, Not Realignment
cards.hook: Working-class voters have been about a third of the American electorate for seventy years. What changed is not their size but their attachment — they left one party without joining the other.

cards.title: Who Gets to Regulate Betting on Elections?
cards.hook: Wisconsin says you can't bet on an election you vote in — a law from 1849. The biggest prediction market calls that 'voter suppression.' Underneath sits a bigger question: which government decides?

cards.title: Why Vote Counts Shift After Election Night
cards.hook: Watch a close race and the leader can flip in the days after polls close. The usual cause is boring — who votes by mail, and when those ballots get counted — not fraud.

cards.title: One Party, Both Chambers, Still No Bill
cards.hook: Republicans hold the White House and both chambers of Congress. A signature voting bill is stuck anyway — a case study in why controlling government isn't the same as controlling the Senate.

cards.title: Can AI Verify a Signature on a Ballot? Experts Say Not Yet
cards.hook: The FBI explored using AI to check signatures on seized mail-in ballots — a case study in what happens when new technology meets an old, imperfect forensic method.

cards.title: What the Election Assistance Commission Does — and Why Its Independence Matters
cards.hook: A little-known federal commission certifies voting machines and helps run U.S. elections. In 2026 the president removed its last sitting members, months before the midterms.

cards.title: What Happens When a Senator's Seat Suddenly Opens Up
cards.hook: When Sen. Lindsey Graham died in office in July 2026, South Carolina didn't call a snap election — it triggered a replacement process most voters never think about until it happens.

cards.title: Mail Ballot Grace Periods
cards.hook: A ballot mailed on Election Day can still arrive days later. Should it count? States disagree — and in 2026 the Supreme Court sided with the states that say yes.

cards.title: Party Spending & Campaign Finance
cards.hook: Since Watergate, a law has capped how much a political party can spend directly coordinating with its own candidate. In 2026 the Supreme Court struck that cap down.

cards.title: Voting Against, Not For
cards.hook: Many voters no longer back a candidate they admire — they vote to keep the other party out. That 'negative partisanship' can make even scandal forgivable.

cards.title: Voting Rights & the Map Fight
cards.hook: The Supreme Court let Alabama use a congressional map a lower court called racially discriminatory — a window into the Voting Rights Act and how redistricting fights reach the Court.

cards.title: How Votes Become Seats
cards.hook: The same ballots can produce very different results depending on the electoral system used to count them.

cards.title: The Discount Airtime Rule — and Who Counts as a Candidate
cards.hook: U.S. law forces broadcasters to sell candidates ad time at their lowest rate near an election. The 2026 fight is not over the discount, but over who gets to claim it.

cards.title: Local Officials Run the Election; Federal Money Defends It
cards.hook: Thousands of county and city offices actually run American elections — but the cyber defense behind them leans on federal money and expertise. When that support pauses, the vulnerability is local.

cards.title: When Two Candidates Agree, the Incumbent Usually Wins
cards.hook: A challenger with nearly the same platform as the incumbent is asking voters to fire someone for no policy reason. That is the hardest race in politics — and it explains long legislative careers.

cards.title: When Organizing Beats Spending
cards.hook: Money buys attention, not turnout. A Florida Senate primary won by the massively outspent candidate is a reminder of what a volunteer ground game can still do.

cards.title: What Counts as Voter ID
cards.hook: A voter ID law is really two decisions: require an ID, then decide which IDs count. The second one quietly determines who gets turned away.

cards.title: When a Lobby Starts Spending on Campaigns
cards.hook: A lobbying group persuades officeholders. A campaign spender helps decide who the officeholders are. Crossing that line changes what a legislator is really being offered.

cards.title: Why Primary Polls Are the Hardest Polls
cards.hook: General-election polling has a stable anchor: party. Primaries strip that anchor away, which is why the same pollsters who do fine in November can miss badly in a primary.

cards.title: What Primary Results Can't Tell You
cards.hook: Every primary night produces a verdict on where a party is headed. The results themselves rarely support one — a handful of low-turnout races is a noisy signal about ideology.

cards.title: What a Party Leader's Endorsement Is Actually Worth
cards.hook: An endorsement is a signal, not an order. Primary voters keep the final say — and sometimes they use it against the person doing the endorsing.

cards.title: Why Some Primaries Need a Second Round
cards.hook: Win 34 percent of a crowded primary and in some states you're the nominee. In others, you go to a runoff — a rule that quietly reshapes which candidates survive.

cards.title: The Reform Almost Nobody Can Name
cards.hook: About 2% of those polled could name proportional representation unprompted. Told what it does, half backed it — opinion on institutions stays latent until someone describes them.

cards.title: Who Decides Which State Votes First?
cards.hook: The order states vote in a presidential nominating contest isn't set by any constitution — it's a party rule, and parties rewrite it to change whose voters get courted first.

cards.title: Proof of Citizenship to Vote
cards.hook: Should you have to show a passport or birth certificate to register to vote? A fight in Congress over that single requirement reveals a deep tension in election design.

cards.title: Maps as Political Power
cards.hook: A map looks like neutral fact, but someone chose what to show, what to leave out, and where to draw the line — and those choices shape voting, travel, and spending.

cards.title: Referendums & Direct Democracy
cards.hook: Usually we elect others to decide for us. Sometimes the people decide a question themselves — that's direct democracy, and the referendum is its main modern tool.

cards.title: The Provisional Ballot: Vote First, Sort It Out Later
cards.hook: The worst way to resolve an eligibility dispute is at the check-in table while the line grows. The provisional ballot exists so you can vote now and let officials verify afterward.

cards.title: The 'Widow's Mandate' and Inherited Political Power
cards.hook: For most of a century, the fastest route for an American woman into Congress was her husband's death. That practice faded — but political inheritance never fully did.

cards.title: How a Legislature Undoes a Ballot Measure Voters Passed
cards.hook: Missouri voters wrote abortion rights into their constitution in 2024. Lawmakers' answer wasn't to defy them — it was to put a second measure, with the same name, back on the ballot.

cards.title: Why Outside Money Loves a Primary
cards.hook: A dollar spent in a low-turnout primary buys far more influence than the same dollar in a general election — which is where super PACs increasingly aim it.

cards.title: The Distinction That Could Reshape Super PACs
cards.hook: Citizens United protects unlimited independent spending. Maine's law doesn't touch spending — it caps what one donor may give the committee doing the spending. That gap is now in court.

cards.title: Declassified Isn't the Same as New
cards.hook: A primetime address, declassified documents, and warnings of 'shocking vulnerabilities' in U.S. elections — but reviewers found the documents mostly repeated what officials already knew years ago.

cards.title: Districts & Gerrymandering
cards.hook: Where you draw the lines on a map can decide an election before a single vote is cast — which is exactly what gerrymandering exploits.

cards.title: When New Maps Force a Second Primary
cards.hook: Redraw a district map after candidates have already filed, and the calendar breaks: some Alabama voters had to nominate candidates twice in one year.

cards.title: Making It Harder to Amend a Constitution — by Amending It First
cards.hook: Some U.S. states are asking voters to approve a measure that would make future constitutional amendments harder to pass. It's direct democracy voting to limit direct democracy.

cards.title: The Census Decides How Many Seats You Get
cards.hook: A once-a-decade headcount sets each state's share of the House for ten years. A Florida challenge argues the count was done wrong — and shows why that is nearly impossible to fix afterward.

cards.title: Racial Vote Dilution: When District Lines Split a Community
cards.hook: Redrawing a map can quietly weaken a racial group's vote — split one community across enough districts and it may elect no one, even where its numbers are large.

cards.title: The Left–Right Spectrum
cards.hook: "Left" and "right" are political shorthand the whole world uses — but they began as nothing more than which side of a room people sat on.

cards.title: Why a Handful of Members Can Stall a Whole Agenda
cards.hook: In a legislature with a thin majority, a bloc of a dozen members who vote together holds a veto — which is why intra-party factions often matter more than the other party does.

cards.hook: Modern parties look powerful on television and weak up close — most have little real control over who runs under their banner. That gap is what lets outsider candidates walk in and take over.

cards.hook: Some of the most important campaign money in Congress doesn't come from voters or donors — it flows between lawmakers themselves, and it quietly buys power.

cards.title: Populism
cards.hook: Populism isn't a single program — it's a style that splits society into two camps: a virtuous 'people' against a corrupt 'elite,' with the populist speaking for the people.

cards.title: Dealignment, Not Realignment
cards.hook: Working-class voters have been about a third of the American electorate for seventy years. What changed is not their size but their attachment — they left one party without joining the other.

cards.title: What Public Policy Is
cards.hook: Passing a law is just the start. Public policy is the whole arc — from defining a problem to actually delivering a solution and seeing whether it worked.

cards.title: The Housing Policy That Sits Between a Shelter and a Home
cards.hook: Building apartments takes years. Emergency shelters help for a night. Tiny house villages spread because they fit the gap — and because local rules allow them faster.

cards.title: Did Troops Cut D.C. Crime?
cards.hook: A new study found the National Guard's deployment in Washington, D.C. had no measurable effect on violent crime — a case study in evaluating public-safety policy with evidence.

cards.title: Deregulation Without Repealing Anything
cards.hook: You do not need to repeal a consumer protection law to switch it off. Stop investigating, ask companies nicely, and take their word for it — the statute stays on the books, unenforced.

cards.title: The Stopgap: Governing by Deadline
cards.hook: Legislatures are supposed to pass budgets. When they cannot agree, many just extend last year's spending a few months at a time — and the deadline becomes the real negotiation.

cards.title: Two Doors to the Same Public Money
cards.hook: A school Texas rejected as a charter got approved for taxpayer-funded vouchers months later. Same money, same state, different door — and a far lower bar.

cards.title: When Locking People Up Is the Local Jobs Plan
cards.hook: Rural places have sold prison beds to distant governments since the 1800s. Immigration detention has revived the trade — and with it an economy that grows only when enforcement does.

cards.title: The Exemption That Hides a Billion Dollars
cards.hook: Oregon publishes what it spends on affordable housing. What it won't publish is what the money bought — an exemption written into its records law in 1997, and almost nobody voted against it.

cards.title: The Trillion-Dollar Budget No One Can Fully Trace
cards.hook: Oversight needs a paper trail. ProPublica's look at U.S. defense spending finds the largest single pot of federal money is also the hardest to follow — and has never passed a full audit.

cards.title: The $533 Million Factory That Made Nothing
cards.hook: Government pays for defense capacity as it is built, not after it works. When the plant never produces, the taxpayer has already footed the bill.

cards.title: What an Executive Order Can and Cannot Change
cards.hook: A presidential order can tell the executive branch what to aim for. It can't skip the process an agency must follow — which is why headlines and reality often diverge.

cards.title: When Detention Is a Revenue Line
cards.hook: Contract out a coercive government function and you create a company whose earnings rise with enforcement — and whose shareholders now have a stake in how the policy goes.

cards.title: Firing an Official Can Require a Hearing First
cards.hook: The fight over removing a Federal Reserve governor turned on something narrower than presidential power: whether she gets told the charge and a chance to answer before she is out.

cards.title: Tariffs Aimed at Behavior, Not Just Trade
cards.hook: A new round of U.S. tariffs was justified not as shielding domestic industry but as punishing countries for weak enforcement of forced-labor bans — trade policy used as a lever on someone else's laws.

cards.title: Who Really Controls Grant Money
cards.hook: The legislature appropriates the money, but the executive writes the rules for handing it out. A proposed U.S. rule would let officials end a federal grant 'at any time, for any reason.'

cards.title: Public Money, Private Oversight: The Voucher Accountability Gap
cards.hook: Public schools face extensive state regulation. Private schools funded by the same taxpayer dollars, through vouchers, often don't — a gap one Arkansas case exposed starkly.

cards.title: Taxation & Public Budgets
cards.hook: A government's budget is its values written in numbers — and taxation is how it raises the money to act at all. Follow the money to understand the priorities.

cards.title: The Welfare State
cards.hook: Should the state guarantee a floor below which no one can fall? The welfare state is modern government's answer — and one of its biggest, most-debated commitments.

cards.title: When a Flood Buyout Can't Reach the People Who Flooded
cards.hook: Disaster buyouts retire dangerous land by purchasing homes. If the residents rent a lot and own a trailer classified as personal property, there is often nothing for the program to buy.

cards.title: When a Policy Reversal Becomes an Experiment
cards.hook: A city banned needle exchange, then a court reinstated it. That accident handed researchers something rare in policy debate — a before-and-after test of the predicted harm.

cards.title: The Study Its Own University Asked to Have Retracted
cards.hook: A university audit found a celebrated study had no ethics approval and unverifiable data. Three years later the journal answered with a 78-word correction — and the study kept guiding care.

cards.title: Protected by a Rule, Not by a Law
cards.hook: Whatever one administration can create with a regulation, the next can undo with a regulation. The move to reopen roadless national forests to logging shows how thin that kind of protection is.

cards.title: Zoning as a Housing Policy Lever: the "Missing Middle"
cards.hook: Nearly 70% of Denver's residential land allows only single-family houses. A simulator estimates that letting four units build anywhere would raise market-rate multifamily supply 46%.

cards.title: When a Private School Is 100% Publicly Funded
cards.hook: Some private schools get every dollar of their tuition from taxpayers — yet the conflict-of-interest, open-records, and open-meeting rules that come with public money don't follow it in.

cards.title: What Happens After a Court Voids a Tax
cards.hook: Courts can strike down a tax — but the money is already collected and spent. The unwinding of one tariff program has reached about $100 billion in refunds, and it is far from finished.

cards.title: When the Visiting Room Goes Video-Only
cards.hook: A jail policy that looks like a small administrative choice — swap in-person visits for paid video calls — runs straight into what the research says keeps people from reoffending.

cards.title: Dangerous, But Not Dangerous Enough to Fix
cards.hook: Omaha yards can hold enough lead to harm a child and still fail to qualify for cleanup — because the rule that decides who gets help was written to a 1994 understanding of the risk.

cards.title: What Happens When a Country Defunds Its Public Broadcaster
cards.hook: A year after the U.S. ended six decades of federal support for public media, the stations are still on air — but the mix of who pays for them, and which ones survive, has changed.

cards.title: Taking Your Land for Someone Else's Server Farm
cards.hook: The Fifth Amendment lets the government take private land for 'public use' with just compensation. Does a power line built to feed one company's data center count?

cards.title: The Great Lakes Program Both Parties Keep Funding
cards.hook: Since 2010 the U.S. has spent over $5 billion cleaning up the Great Lakes — and it has survived Congress after Congress. The coalition behind it is a case study in building bipartisan support.

cards.title: Why Parties Write Governing Plans Before They Win
cards.hook: Long before an election, the out-of-power side is often already drafting exactly what it would do if it won — a governing blueprint built to be ready on day one.

cards.title: State Constitutions Can Guarantee More Than the Federal One Does
cards.hook: The U.S. Constitution sets a floor of rights, not a ceiling. New York's constitution goes further — it makes aiding the needy a state duty, not just a policy choice.

cards.title: Why It's So Hard to Sue Your Health Insurer
cards.hook: A 1974 law meant to protect pensions also quietly shields most employer health plans from lawsuits over wrongly denied claims — even when the denial causes real harm.

cards.title: Can Carbon Capture Solve Climate Change?
cards.hook: What if we could keep burning fossil fuels and just vacuum the carbon back out? That promise is seductive, politically powerful — and, a major investigation argues, a mirage.

cards.title: Why Census Data Has 'Noise' Added
cards.hook: To stop anyone reverse-engineering your identity from public statistics, the U.S. census deliberately blurs its own numbers — a privacy-for-accuracy trade with real political stakes.

cards.title: Markets, Regulation & the Mixed Economy
cards.hook: Pure free market or full state control? Almost every country picks neither — they run a mixed economy, and where they draw the line is one of politics' great arguments.

cards.title: A Court Can Order Treatment. It Can't Order the Appointment to Exist.
cards.hook: A county can now court-order outpatient mental health treatment — but of 279 Medicaid providers listed, a study found only 34 had open appointments. Legal authority alone doesn't deliver a service.

cards.title: Public Goods & the State
cards.hook: Some things markets struggle to provide — clean air, national defense, street lighting — because no one can be charged for them. That gap is a core reason states exist.

cards.title: What 'Insolvency' Actually Means for a Trust Fund
cards.hook: Most Americans think the Social Security trust fund running out means no checks. It means smaller checks — and the gap between those two beliefs is why the fix keeps getting deferred.

cards.title: You Can Donate to the Government — You Can't Direct It
cards.hook: Private money paying for a public building sounds like a bargain for taxpayers. Under U.S. law it mostly isn't allowed, because the power to decide what government spends belongs to Congress.

cards.title: Regulating Nuclear Power: Speed vs. Safety
cards.hook: Speeding up approval for new nuclear reactors could mean cheaper, faster clean power — or it could mean cutting the safety review that catches problems first. Regulators have to choose.

cards.title: The Free Press & Democracy
cards.hook: A free press is sometimes called the "fourth estate" — an unofficial branch of power whose job is to watch the other three on the public's behalf.

cards.title: Media Trust Is Built Two Ways, Not One
cards.hook: Most fixes for distrust in the press ask journalists to try harder. Research on Black communities in Minneapolis found the overlooked half is whether the community engages back.

cards.title: Prices Vote: Economic Conditions and the Incumbent
cards.hook: Voters rarely audit a governing record line by line. They ask a cruder question — is life more affordable than it was? — and that question moves elections more reliably than most policy debates.

cards.title: Trust Is a Behavior, Not a Credential
cards.hook: Credentials tell you who is qualified. They do not tell anyone whether to act on your advice — and acting on advice, at some risk to yourself, is what trust actually is.

cards.hook: The First Amendment names speech and the press separately — but the Court has folded the press clause into the speech clause, leaving journalists no rights an ordinary blogger lacks.

cards.title: When Speed of Access to Official Speech Is for Sale
cards.hook: A leader's posts move markets and policy. What happens to equal access when a company charges customers to receive them milliseconds sooner?

cards.title: The People With No Opinion

cards.title: Declassified Isn't the Same as New

cards.title: Can the Government Force a Reporter to Reveal a Source?
cards.hook: There's no absolute First Amendment shield protecting a journalist's sources — which is exactly what makes a federal subpoena for reporters' grand jury testimony such a live threat to the free press.

cards.title: Disinformation & Propaganda
cards.hook: Democracy depends on citizens being informed — so deliberately polluting what they know is a direct attack on it. That's the threat of propaganda and disinformation.

cards.title: Deliberation Is a Skill, and It Can Be Designed
cards.hook: Most public meetings are a queue of three-minute speeches at a panel. Deliberative democracy treats talking well as a designed process — with guides, trained facilitators, and no winner declared.

cards.title: Who Are the "Friends of the Court"?
cards.hook: Most briefs a supreme court reads are filed by people who aren't suing anyone. The amicus brief is how outside interests get a say in a case they are not party to.

cards.title: When a 'Candidate' Texting You Is Actually a Bot
cards.hook: Campaigns have always texted voters. Now some of those texts are AI-generated conversations trained to sound like the candidate — personalized, responsive, and not always clearly labeled.

cards.title: Why No Cameras in the Supreme Court?
cards.hook: You can read every Supreme Court ruling, but you can't watch the arguments on video. The long fight over courtroom cameras is really a fight over judicial transparency.

cards.title: The Politics of Spectacle
cards.hook: Bread and circuses, military parades, staged combat — leaders have always used spectacle to project power and bind people to a shared identity.

cards.title: Prediction Markets in Politics

cards.title: Interest Groups & Lobbying

cards.title: Public Opinion & Polling
cards.hook: What 'the people' think shapes what governments do — but measuring it is trickier than it looks, and a bad poll can mislead as easily as a good one informs.

cards.title: Social Movements & Protest
cards.hook: When ordinary channels fail or move too slowly, people organize and take to the streets. Social movements are how the unrepresented push change onto the agenda.

cards.title: Don't Trust the Name on the PAC
cards.hook: The cheapest way to disguise who is talking to voters isn't a lie in the ad — it's a reassuring name on the group paying for it.

cards.hook: A 26-day fast in India drew a national audience and helped ignite a youth movement — then the fast ended and the protests didn't, which is the more telling part.

cards.title: The Expert Who Shapes the Law
cards.hook: Lawmakers regulating a product they do not understand call a scientist. Whether that scientist's travel was paid for by the industry is not a detail — it is the whole reliability question.

cards.title: The Deepfake That Doesn't Have to Fool You Twice
cards.hook: The most effective synthetic video isn't the most realistic one. It's the one that looks like something you already scroll past every day — a talk-show clip about yesterday's news.

cards.title: Betting on What the President Will Say — From Inside the Room
