cards.hook: A lobbying group persuades officeholders. A campaign spender helps decide who the officeholders are. Crossing that line changes what a legislator is really being offered.

cards.title: Why Primary Polls Are the Hardest Polls
cards.hook: General-election polling has a stable anchor: party. Primaries strip that anchor away, which is why the same pollsters who do fine in November can miss badly in a primary.

cards.title: How Opinion on Abortion Shifted After Dobbs
cards.hook: When the Supreme Court returned abortion to the states in 2022, it didn't settle the debate — public opinion moved, with more Americans taking firm pro-access positions.

cards.title: Climate Opinion: Party Matters, But Not the Whole Story
cards.hook: Party predicts how Americans feel about climate — but not the whole story: a young Republican may cheer solar panels and still reject a carbon tax.

cards.title: Do People Trust the Court, or Just Their Side of It?
cards.hook: Only 46% of Americans approve of the Supreme Court overall — but break it down by party, and the real story is a 56-point gap in how Republicans and Democrats see the same institution.

cards.title: The Poll Behind the Headlines: More Agreement Than It Looks
cards.hook: Ask Americans about the country's 250th anniversary and you get a partisan split. Ask about the country's founding ideals and something odd happens: the numbers converge.

cards.title: The Provisional Ballot: Vote First, Sort It Out Later
cards.hook: The worst way to resolve an eligibility dispute is at the check-in table while the line grows. The provisional ballot exists so you can vote now and let officials verify afterward.

cards.title: What Citizenship Is
cards.hook: Citizenship is the formal bond between a person and a state — the status that turns a resident into a full member, with rights and duties to match.

cards.title: The 'Widow's Mandate' and Inherited Political Power
cards.hook: For most of a century, the fastest route for an American woman into Congress was her husband's death. That practice faded — but political inheritance never fully did.

cards.title: You Don't Have to Live in the District You Represent
cards.hook: The Constitution asks a House candidate to be an inhabitant of the state — not the district. That gap is why 'carpetbagger' is an insult and not a disqualification.

cards.title: The Hunger Strike, and What Outlives It
cards.hook: A 26-day fast in India drew a national audience and helped ignite a youth movement — then the fast ended and the protests didn't, which is the more telling part.

cards.title: Birthright Citizenship & the 14th Amendment
cards.hook: Born on U.S. soil, you're a citizen — full stop, according to the Constitution's plain text. In 2026 the Supreme Court reaffirmed that even a presidential order can't rewrite it.

cards.title: Trust Is a Behavior, Not a Credential
cards.hook: Credentials tell you who is qualified. They do not tell anyone whether to act on your advice — and acting on advice, at some risk to yourself, is what trust actually is.

cards.title: Why Noncitizen Voting Cases Are Hard to Prosecute
cards.hook: A rule can be clear and the enforcement still collapse. Charging noncitizens with voting means proving they knew they were ineligible — and that is where the cases fall apart.

cards.title: Losing in Court Isn't Always the End of a Policy
cards.hook: A court judgment binds the order in front of it. Rewrite the order and the clock restarts at the bottom of the judicial ladder — sometimes for years.

cards.title: Self-Regulation and the Jurisdiction Gap
cards.hook: When a private body governs an activity but sits outside every regulator's remit, weak rules stop being a flaw and start being a competitive advantage.

cards.title: How Parades and Festivals Redefine 'One of Us'
cards.hook: A Lunar New Year 5K, a Fourth of July parade with a woman in a sari, a festival that reclaims a slur — public celebrations quietly redraw who counts as a full member of the community.

cards.title: Proof of Citizenship to Vote
cards.hook: Should you have to show a passport or birth certificate to register to vote? A fight in Congress over that single requirement reveals a deep tension in election design.

cards.title: Temporary Protected Status
cards.hook: Some immigrants are allowed to stay not because they won asylum, but because their home country is too dangerous to return to — for now. That 'for now' is the whole idea.

cards.title: Immigration & Naturalization
cards.hook: Every state has to answer two charged questions: who gets to come in, and who gets to become one of us? That's the politics of immigration and citizenship.

cards.title: Ways to Participate
cards.hook: Voting is the headline act of citizenship — but it's only one of many ways people shape politics, from joining a party to signing a petition or marching.

cards.title: Voter Turnout & Engagement
cards.hook: Who shows up changes who wins. Turnout — the share of eligible people who actually vote — is one of the quiet forces shaping every election.

cards.title: A Visa Is Permission, Not a Right
cards.hook: A visa does not entitle anyone to stay — it is a revocable permission to ask to be let in. That legal detail is why mass revocations can happen with a signature.

cards.title: Deliberation Is a Skill, and It Can Be Designed
cards.hook: Most public meetings are a queue of three-minute speeches at a panel. Deliberative democracy treats talking well as a designed process — with guides, trained facilitators, and no winner declared.

cards.title: Political Corruption
cards.hook: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain — and it quietly drains a society, eroding trust, fairness, and the resources meant for everyone.

cards.title: A Speedy Remedy That Isn't Speedy
cards.hook: Habeas corpus lets a detained person ask a judge one question: is this lawful? The protection depends on getting an answer quickly — and ProPublica found some judges take months.

cards.title: The Expert Who Shapes the Law
cards.hook: Lawmakers regulating a product they do not understand call a scientist. Whether that scientist's travel was paid for by the industry is not a detail — it is the whole reliability question.

cards.title: Two Doors to the Same Public Money
cards.hook: A school Texas rejected as a charter got approved for taxpayer-funded vouchers months later. Same money, same state, different door — and a far lower bar.

cards.title: The Office Whose Job Is Counting the Wrong Deaths
cards.hook: Militaries do not automatically learn from killing civilians. Somebody has to be paid to investigate it, and that office can be closed as easily as it was opened.

cards.title: A Time Limit Only Binds If Someone Counts the Clock
cards.hook: A 72-hour cap on holding someone sounds like a hard limit. It is only as hard as the rule about when the count starts over.

cards.title: The One-Justice Order That Freezes a Case
cards.hook: Before the Supreme Court decides anything, a single justice can push pause. That's how White House ballroom construction kept going after two lower courts had ordered it stopped.

cards.title: How Official Statistics Earn Trust
cards.hook: A government statistic carries weight only because of the process behind it. When a report skips the usual methodology and review, the number stops being evidence and becomes an argument.

cards.title: Why Outside Money Loves a Primary
cards.hook: A dollar spent in a low-turnout primary buys far more influence than the same dollar in a general election — which is where super PACs increasingly aim it.

cards.title: When the State Contracts Out Custody, Oversight Doesn't Follow
cards.hook: Governments can delegate the job of locking someone up. What often fails to travel with the contract is the duty to open the records.

cards.title: The Distinction That Could Reshape Super PACs
cards.hook: Citizens United protects unlimited independent spending. Maine's law doesn't touch spending — it caps what one donor may give the committee doing the spending. That gap is now in court.

cards.title: The Presumption of Regularity
cards.hook: Courts normally start by assuming the government followed its own rules and told the truth. That default is quiet, load-bearing — and, judges are now saying out loud, forfeitable.

cards.title: Mission Creep: When a Body Outgrows Its Stated Job
cards.hook: Memphis got a federal task force announced to fight violent crime. Ten months on, it had driven a surge of immigration arrests — mostly of people with no convictions. A study in how missions drift.

cards.title: Who Really Controls Grant Money
cards.hook: The legislature appropriates the money, but the executive writes the rules for handing it out. A proposed U.S. rule would let officials end a federal grant 'at any time, for any reason.'

cards.title: The Pardon Isn't for Sale. The Advocacy Is.
cards.hook: Paying for a presidential pardon outright would be a crime. Paying someone up to $5 million to get you in front of the president to ask for one? Perfectly legal — and a growing D.C. industry.

cards.title: Betting on What the President Will Say — From Inside the Room
cards.hook: Prediction markets let anyone bet on politics. A White House staffer allegedly used his own front-row seat to Trump's speeches to place winning bets on Trump's own words.

cards.title: Public Money, Private Oversight: The Voucher Accountability Gap
cards.hook: Public schools face extensive state regulation. Private schools funded by the same taxpayer dollars, through vouchers, often don't — a gap one Arkansas case exposed starkly.

cards.title: What the Election Assistance Commission Does — and Why Its Independence Matters
cards.hook: A little-known federal commission certifies voting machines and helps run U.S. elections. In 2026 the president removed its last sitting members, months before the midterms.

cards.title: The Supreme Court's 'Shadow Docket'
cards.hook: Most Supreme Court rulings today aren't fully-argued opinions — they're fast, often unsigned orders with little explanation. In the term ending October 2025, those quietly became the majority.

cards.title: Accountability & Oversight
cards.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

cards.title: Censure: Punishment Without Removal
cards.hook: Legislatures mostly cannot fire their own members easily — voters hired them. So they built a middle sanction: a formal, recorded statement that the chamber disapproves.

cards.title: Why the Out-Party Runs on Corruption
cards.hook: Democrats mentioned corruption six times as often in 2026 constituent emails as in 2022. That jump says less about new scandals than about what corruption does for a party with no power to legislate.

cards.title: "Clearly Established" Law and Qualified Immunity
cards.hook: A right you hold on paper can be unenforceable in court: officials escape damages unless a prior ruling already said, in nearly identical facts, that what they did was illegal.

cards.title: The Study Its Own University Asked to Have Retracted
cards.hook: A university audit found a celebrated study had no ethics approval and unverifiable data. Three years later the journal answered with a 78-word correction — and the study kept guiding care.

cards.title: A Strict Privacy Law Is Only as Strong as Its Enforcer
cards.hook: A state can write the toughest data privacy law in the country and still see the data sold. Rights on paper need someone whose job is to notice when they're ignored.

cards.title: When the Complaint Box Is the Only Oversight
cards.hook: Give people in custody a form to file complaints and you can call it oversight. If nobody outside answers it, the next step isn't another form — it's a hunger strike.

cards.title: When the Agency Investigates Its Critics
cards.hook: A man emailed criticism to the head of ICE. Agents later tracked him to his house, the airport and a hotel to ask about it. The knock itself is the constitutional problem.

cards.title: Who Decides Which Charities Get the Money?
cards.hook: A donor-advised fund gives the tax break the day money goes in — but the money legally belongs to the sponsor, and the sponsor decides which charities may receive it.

cards.title: When a Private School Is 100% Publicly Funded
cards.hook: Some private schools get every dollar of their tuition from taxpayers — yet the conflict-of-interest, open-records, and open-meeting rules that come with public money don't follow it in.

cards.title: Three Kinds of Denial That Let Institutions Off the Hook
cards.hook: Sociologist Stanley Cohen built a typology to explain how societies wave away state atrocities. It turns out to describe how any institution protects its own — one denial at a time.

cards.title: Cynicism Is the Enemy of Reform
cards.hook: Large majorities call the political system corrupt, across party lines. But some voters read the facts as outrageous and others as just how things work — and that split decides if anything changes.

cards.title: Who Checks Whether a Cleanup Held?
cards.hook: The EPA remediated 13,000 Omaha yards and moved on. Reporters retested 620 of them for $10 a sample — and found lead above the agency's own trigger in four of every ten.

cards.title: Exonerated Isn't the Same as Compensated
cards.hook: Getting a conviction thrown out does not get you paid. In most states you must then prove your innocence all over again — to a higher standard, against a state that may still call you guilty.

cards.title: The Cap on What Judges Can Earn on the Side
cards.hook: Federal judges may only earn a few tens of thousands of dollars outside the job — a rule meant to keep outside money from buying influence. Writing books is one of the carve-outs.

cards.title: Not All Dissents Are Created Equal
cards.hook: Dissent tallies treat a one-line 'I would deny' the same as a fully reasoned opinion. One scholar sorted 386 of them on the emergency docket — and found about half were just bare votes.

cards.title: The Internet Subsidy Program Paying to Wire Empty Buildings
cards.hook: Phone customers nationwide pay over $340,000 a year to keep a nearly-abandoned Alaska island 'wired' for slow internet — while the few people who actually live there just use Starlink.

cards.title: How a Federal Agency Changes Its Own Rules — No New Law Required
cards.hook: After a string of deadly shootings tied to its officers, ICE didn't wait for Congress to act. It just changed its own internal policy — a reminder of how much agencies can do on their own.

cards.title: There's No 25th Amendment for Congress
cards.hook: When a president is incapacitated, the Constitution has a formal fix: the 25th Amendment. When a senator is hospitalized for weeks with no details given, there isn't one.

cards.title: When a Gun-Permit Decision Becomes a Federal Civil Rights Case
cards.hook: A city police department can revoke a concealed-carry license for 'good cause.' Who that standard gets applied to is what can turn it into a federal civil rights investigation.

cards.title: Rulemaking Is Supposed to Include the Public — What Happens When It Doesn't
cards.hook: Before a federal agency can change a regulation, it's normally required to ask the public first. A 2026 overhaul of grazing rules on federal land tested how easily that step can be trimmed.

cards.title: Why Supreme Court Justices Have to Show Their Books
cards.hook: Federal judges don't campaign for office or face voters — so how does the public keep tabs on their outside income, gifts, and travel? One tool: a legally required annual disclosure.

cards.title: Consent Decrees & Police Oversight
cards.hook: When a police department is found to systematically violate rights, the usual fix is a federal consent decree — a court-enforced reform plan. What happens when the enforcer stops enforcing?

cards.title: Regulatory Capture
cards.hook: Who protects a city's drinking water when the industry that put it at risk is also the one the regulator was built to serve? That's the problem political scientists call regulatory capture.

cards.title: When Judges Step Aside
cards.hook: A judge who might be biased is supposed to step aside. But on the U.S. Supreme Court, each justice decides that alone — and no one can overrule them.

cards.title: How Lawmakers Fund Each Other
cards.hook: Some of the most important campaign money in Congress doesn't come from voters or donors — it flows between lawmakers themselves, and it quietly buys power.

cards.title: Freedom of Information
cards.hook: You can't hold power to account for what you can't see. Freedom of information laws pry open the workings of government so citizens can actually check it.

cards.title: The Civil Service & Bureaucracy
cards.hook: Governments change; the bureaucracy stays. The permanent civil service is the machinery that actually delivers policy — for better and, sometimes, for worse.

cards.title: Deregulation Without Repealing Anything
cards.hook: You do not need to repeal a consumer protection law to switch it off. Stop investigating, ask companies nicely, and take their word for it — the statute stays on the books, unenforced.

cards.title: Scientific Integrity Policies Are Only Words Until Tested
cards.hook: Agencies that produce official numbers usually have a written rule barring political interference. It is an internal policy — which means the same agency can edit it.

cards.title: Who Decides What to Charge
cards.hook: A prosecutor builds a case; headquarters picks the charge. That chain of command is normal — and it is also the point where a case can be quietly downgraded.

cards.title: The Side Door Into a Closed Facility
cards.hook: Journalists can't get inside an immigration detention camp. But when the camp dials 911, the call lands in a county system — where public records law still applies.

cards.title: When Officials Sign an NDA
cards.hook: A nondisclosure agreement is a private contract. When public officials sign one, the public loses its normal claim on what its own government is negotiating.

cards.title: The Exemption That Hides a Billion Dollars
cards.hook: Oregon publishes what it spends on affordable housing. What it won't publish is what the money bought — an exemption written into its records law in 1997, and almost nobody voted against it.

cards.title: The Trillion-Dollar Budget No One Can Fully Trace
cards.hook: Oversight needs a paper trail. ProPublica's look at U.S. defense spending finds the largest single pot of federal money is also the hardest to follow — and has never passed a full audit.

cards.title: The $533 Million Factory That Made Nothing
cards.hook: Government pays for defense capacity as it is built, not after it works. When the plant never produces, the taxpayer has already footed the bill.

cards.title: Self-Regulation and the Jurisdiction Gap
cards.hook: When a private body governs an activity but sits outside every regulator's remit, weak rules stop being a flaw and start being a competitive advantage.

cards.title: A Reform Gets Promised. Then What?
cards.hook: DHS promised body cameras for every immigration agent after a fatal shooting. Six months later, two more people are dead — and still no cameras.

cards.title: Gifts, Regulators, and the Companies They Regulate
cards.hook: Two FCC officials took pricey gala tickets from Paramount while the company had billions of dollars in mergers awaiting the agency's approval. Ethics rules exist for exactly this.

cards.title: When the Defendant Helps Decide What Evidence You Get
cards.hook: A subpoena went to the city police, not the university. The university stepped in anyway to argue it was too broad — and won the right to help sort which files count.

cards.title: The Weak Point of Transparency Law: Silence
cards.hook: A records law doesn't have to be repealed to stop working. An agency can simply not answer — and the only remedy left is a lawsuit most requesters can't afford.

cards.title: Civil Liberties Basics
cards.hook: The freedoms that protect individuals from overreach by the state — like speech, belief, and a fair trial.

cards.title: Freedom of Expression
cards.hook: The freedom to speak, publish, and dissent is often called the first freedom — because without it, citizens can't check power or argue their way to better decisions.

cards.title: Consent Is the Biggest Exception
cards.hook: A warrantless search of a home is presumptively unreasonable — unless you say yes. And nobody is required to tell you that you may say no.

cards.title: The Beating That Asked: Is Some Speech Itself Violence?
cards.hook: In 1856, a congressman beat a senator unconscious with a cane over an anti-slavery speech — and forced America to argue over whether words can be treated as an act of violence.

cards.title: Birthright Citizenship & the 14th Amendment
cards.hook: Born on U.S. soil, you're a citizen — full stop, according to the Constitution's plain text. In 2026 the Supreme Court reaffirmed that even a presidential order can't rewrite it.

cards.title: A Right With No Way to Sue Is Half a Right
cards.hook: A prisoner's religious rights were violated and the harm was already done. The hard legal question was not whether it was wrong — it was whether he could recover anything at all.

cards.title: When the Law Carves Out an Exception for Belief
cards.hook: Idaho parents can decline medical care for a sick child on religious grounds and be shielded from prosecution. That exemption is not ancient — a federal funding rule helped create it.

cards.title: The First Amendment Clause That Stopped Doing Any Work
cards.hook: The First Amendment names speech and the press separately — but the Court has folded the press clause into the speech clause, leaving journalists no rights an ordinary blogger lacks.

cards.title: A Time Limit Only Binds If Someone Counts the Clock
cards.hook: A 72-hour cap on holding someone sounds like a hard limit. It is only as hard as the rule about when the count starts over.

cards.title: How a Legislature Undoes a Ballot Measure Voters Passed
cards.hook: Missouri voters wrote abortion rights into their constitution in 2024. Lawmakers' answer wasn't to defy them — it was to put a second measure, with the same name, back on the ballot.

cards.title: When a Precedent Loses Its Foundation
cards.hook: A 1980 ruling barred the Ten Commandments from public classrooms. An appeals court says the test it rested on is gone — so the ruling is too. That claim is now at the Supreme Court.

cards.title: When the State Contracts Out Custody, Oversight Doesn't Follow
cards.hook: Governments can delegate the job of locking someone up. What often fails to travel with the contract is the duty to open the records.

cards.title: The Constitutional Court of South Africa
cards.hook: Born out of the end of apartheid, this court was designed to make a new constitution stick — and became one of the world's most-cited voices on what rights a government owes its people.

cards.title: Racial Vote Dilution: When District Lines Split a Community
cards.hook: Redrawing a map can quietly weaken a racial group's vote — split one community across enough districts and it may elect no one, even where its numbers are large.

cards.title: The Memo Congress Never Voted On
cards.hook: A presidential memorandum can direct 200-plus FBI task forces to hunt down a whole ideology — no bill, no vote, and no requirement it even be made public.

cards.title: Geofence Warrants & the Fourth Amendment
cards.hook: Police can ask a tech company which phones were near a crime scene at a given hour — sweeping up everyone's location, not just a suspect's. In 2026 the Court said that's a 'search.'

cards.title: Abortion After Dobbs
cards.hook: In 2022 the Supreme Court did something rare: it withdrew a constitutional right it had recognized for half a century — and handed the question back to the states.

cards.title: The Eighth Amendment & Methods of Execution
cards.hook: The Constitution bars 'cruel and unusual' punishment — so courts must decide not only whether a state may execute, but whether the method it chooses is constitutional.

cards.title: FISA Section 702
cards.hook: The law behind much of America's foreign-intelligence collection — powerful enough to feed most of the president's daily brief, yet it expires unless Congress keeps renewing it.

cards.title: The Right to Bear Arms
cards.hook: How does a court decide which weapons are protected? The U.S. Supreme Court's answer turns on a deceptively simple phrase: arms 'in common use.'

cards.title: Trying Children as Adults
cards.hook: Most legal systems treat young offenders differently — on the logic that a still-developing brain can change. So why are some children still tried in adult courts?

cards.title: Voting Rights & the Map Fight
cards.hook: The Supreme Court let Alabama use a congressional map a lower court called racially discriminatory — a window into the Voting Rights Act and how redistricting fights reach the Court.

cards.title: Due Process
cards.hook: Due process is the promise that the state can't take your liberty or property on a whim — it must follow fair, known rules before it acts against you.

cards.title: Equality & Minority Rights
cards.hook: Majority rule can become majority tyranny. Equality before the law and minority rights are how democracies stop the many from trampling the few.

cards.title: When the Defendant Helps Decide What Evidence You Get
cards.hook: A subpoena went to the city police, not the university. The university stepped in anyway to argue it was too broad — and won the right to help sort which files count.

cards.title: Why Bail Is Rare in Extradition Cases
cards.hook: Bail turns on one question: will this person come back? Extradition cases are the setting where courts trust that answer least.

cards.title: The Supreme Court's Other Docket
cards.hook: The Court hears about sixty argued cases a year and disposes of thousands more by short written order. Most of what it does never gets an opinion at all.

cards.title: "Clearly Established" Law and Qualified Immunity
cards.hook: A right you hold on paper can be unenforceable in court: officials escape damages unless a prior ruling already said, in nearly identical facts, that what they did was illegal.

cards.title: Is Calling Something 'The Big Lie' an Opinion?
cards.hook: Defamation law protects opinion but not false facts — so the whole fight is over which side of that line a phrase falls on. Trump's suit against CNN asks the Supreme Court to redraw it.

cards.title: When the Agency Investigates Its Critics
cards.hook: A man emailed criticism to the head of ICE. Agents later tracked him to his house, the airport and a hotel to ask about it. The knock itself is the constitutional problem.

cards.title: What Counts as Voter ID
cards.hook: A voter ID law is really two decisions: require an ID, then decide which IDs count. The second one quietly determines who gets turned away.

cards.title: How Extradition Works
cards.hook: One country asking another to hand over a person is not a favor between friends — it runs on treaties and courts, and political goodwill is not the deciding vote.

cards.title: When the Constitution Says Nothing Yet
cards.hook: About 96,000 American children were born through IVF in 2023. The Supreme Court has barely addressed the technology — leaving state courts to invent the rules one dispute at a time.

cards.title: How Many Jurors Make a Jury?
cards.hook: Everyone pictures twelve. But in 1970 the Supreme Court called that number a 'historical accident' — and now it has agreed to look again.

cards.title: Tribal Nations as a Third Sovereign
cards.hook: American federalism is usually taught as states versus Washington. That leaves out hundreds of tribal governments whose authority predates the Constitution itself.

cards.title: When the Visiting Room Goes Video-Only
cards.hook: A jail policy that looks like a small administrative choice — swap in-person visits for paid video calls — runs straight into what the research says keeps people from reoffending.

cards.title: Exonerated Isn't the Same as Compensated
cards.hook: Getting a conviction thrown out does not get you paid. In most states you must then prove your innocence all over again — to a higher standard, against a state that may still call you guilty.

cards.title: Terrorism Charges Without an Ideology
cards.hook: Texas is prosecuting a teenage shooting spree as terrorism with no manifesto and no extremist ties — testing whether the crime is defined by motive or by the fear it creates.

cards.title: How Opinion on Abortion Shifted After Dobbs
cards.hook: When the Supreme Court returned abortion to the states in 2022, it didn't settle the debate — public opinion moved, with more Americans taking firm pro-access positions.

cards.title: Taking Your Land for Someone Else's Server Farm
cards.hook: The Fifth Amendment lets the government take private land for 'public use' with just compensation. Does a power line built to feed one company's data center count?

cards.title: Whose Park Is It, Anyway?
cards.hook: Lafayette Square has hosted protests aimed at the White House for generations. A proposal for a permanent 8-to-9-foot fence around it puts security and free assembly on a literal collision course.

cards.title: When a Gun-Permit Decision Becomes a Federal Civil Rights Case
cards.hook: A city police department can revoke a concealed-carry license for 'good cause.' Who that standard gets applied to is what can turn it into a federal civil rights investigation.

cards.title: State Constitutions Can Guarantee More Than the Federal One Does
cards.hook: The U.S. Constitution sets a floor of rights, not a ceiling. New York's constitution goes further — it makes aiding the needy a state duty, not just a policy choice.

cards.title: When DNA Evidence Outlasts the Statute of Limitations
cards.hook: A crime can go unprosecuted forever once its statute of limitations runs out — even if DNA later identifies a suspect. Massachusetts is one of the last states moving to close that gap.

cards.title: The Right to Understand Your Trial
cards.hook: A trial you can't understand isn't a fair one — so the law promises defendants an interpreter. For speakers of rarer languages, that promise often goes unmet.

cards.title: Civil Liberties vs Civil Rights
cards.hook: Two terms people mix up: liberties are freedoms from government interference; rights are protections to be treated equally.

cards.title: Where a 'Right to Privacy' Comes From
cards.hook: The word 'privacy' never appears in the U.S. Constitution. Decades of doctrine hang on where courts decided to find it — and a long-running argument says they looked in the wrong place.

cards.title: The Constitution Has Clauses Courts Won't Touch
cards.hook: Not every line in the Constitution gets fought over in court. Some, like the ban on quartering soldiers, have sat almost untouched for over two centuries — by choice, not by accident.

cards.title: A Speedy Remedy That Isn't Speedy
cards.hook: Habeas corpus lets a detained person ask a judge one question: is this lawful? The protection depends on getting an answer quickly — and ProPublica found some judges take months.

cards.title: How Much Deference Does the Military Get?
cards.hook: Courts scrutinize government classifications closely — except in the military, where judges have long deferred. A transgender service ban now tests where that deference stops.

cards.title: When Detention Conditions Become a Pressure Tactic
cards.hook: Immigration detention is supposed to hold people while their case is decided — not persuade them to give up on it. Reporting from inside a Texas facility raises exactly that question.

cards.title: Junk Science & Wrongful Conviction
cards.hook: A courtroom isn't a lab — but it has to rely on forensic science anyway. When that science turns out to be unreliable, the wrong person can spend years, or a life, on death row.

cards.title: Transgender Athletes & Equal Protection
cards.hook: Can a state law treat male and female athletes differently and still satisfy the Constitution's promise of equal treatment? In 2026 the Supreme Court said yes, for school sports.

cards.title: Sovereignty Among Nations
cards.hook: Inside its borders a state is supreme — but in the world of states there's no higher ruler. That gap, called anarchy, shapes everything about international politics.

cards.title: Who Gets to Decide What Goes on a Map
cards.hook: Renaming a lake is not a matter of announcing it. In the U.S. a name normally climbs from town to county to state to a federal board — and stops entirely at the border.

cards.title: The 1789 Law That Let the World Sue in U.S. Courts
cards.hook: One sentence written by the first Congress quietly became America's main door for human rights lawsuits — and the Supreme Court has spent two decades narrowing it.

cards.title: Even a Superpower Can't Just Order a Sovereign Country to Comply
cards.hook: The U.S. indicted Mexican officials on drug-corruption charges and threatened economic penalties. Mexico's president said no anyway — a case study in the real limits of sovereignty.

cards.title: A Pattern Two Centuries Old: Backing the Opposition, Denying It Officially
cards.hook: In 1805 a Venezuelan revolutionary asked Jefferson for help overthrowing Spanish rule. Jefferson denied involvement but quietly let him go — a pattern historians trace to 2026.

cards.title: The European Court of Justice
cards.hook: A court above nations: it doesn't replace any country's supreme court, but it makes sure EU law means the same thing in every member state.

cards.title: Diplomacy & War
cards.hook: States pursue their interests on a spectrum that runs from the conference table to the battlefield. Diplomacy and war are two ends of the same toolkit.

cards.title: Treaties & International Law
cards.hook: If no world government can pass laws, how do nations bind themselves at all? Largely by agreeing to — treaties are the contracts that knit the international order together.

cards.title: The UN & International Organizations
cards.hook: Sovereign states that answer to no one above them still build standing clubs to cooperate. The UN is the largest — a forum, not a world government.

cards.title: Why a Big Resource Deal Doesn't Move the Price at the Pump
cards.hook: Governments announce access to vast oil reserves and imply cheaper fuel. Oil in the ground and barrels on the market are separated by years of capital, and by a global price.

cards.title: Why Bail Is Rare in Extradition Cases
cards.hook: Bail turns on one question: will this person come back? Extradition cases are the setting where courts trust that answer least.

cards.title: Giving a Country Weapons vs. Teaching It to Build Them
cards.hook: Shipping missiles buys a partner time. Sharing the blueprints changes what it can do without you — which is why technology transfer is a bigger decision than any single delivery.

cards.title: Readiness Is a Reserve You Spend
cards.hook: A carrier's record 266-day deployment isn't a story about a weak military. It's a story about a budget nobody tracks: the finite reserve of crew rest and maintenance that every deployment draws down.

cards.title: When Economic Statecraft Stops Biting
cards.hook: Tariffs and export controls are the two big levers of economic security policy. Both have a habit of losing force the longer they stay pulled.

cards.title: Why Tariff Fights Escalate
cards.hook: The U.S. put 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods; Canada said within hours it would hit back. That reflex — retaliate, don't absorb — is what turns a tariff into a trade war.

cards.title: How Extradition Works
cards.hook: One country asking another to hand over a person is not a favor between friends — it runs on treaties and courts, and political goodwill is not the deciding vote.

cards.title: Why Ceasefires Break Down
cards.hook: A ceasefire stops the shooting. It does not make peace. The difference — and the danger — lies in everything a quick deal leaves out.

cards.title: 30x30 and the 'Paper Park' Problem
cards.hook: The world pledged to protect 30% of the ocean by 2030. But a line on a map isn't protection — and much of what's been promised exists only on paper.

cards.title: Precautionary Diplomacy
cards.hook: Most treaties clean up a mess after it happens. A rarer kind acts first — banning commercial fishing in the Arctic before it even begins, to buy time for science.

cards.title: Soft Power & Hard Power
cards.hook: States get their way two ways: by force and money, or by attraction. Knowing the difference between hard power and soft power explains a lot about how influence really works.

cards.title: Theories of International Relations
cards.hook: Why do states behave as they do? Three big theories give rival answers — and which lens you use changes what you see in every global event.

cards.title: Sanctions: The Weapon States Reach For Before They Reach For Weapons
cards.hook: Cutting a country off from money and markets sits between a strongly-worded letter and a war — which is exactly why governments use it so often, and why it so often disappoints.

cards.title: What Human Rights Are
cards.hook: Human rights are the radical claim that every person — regardless of country, status, or who's in charge — holds certain basic rights simply by being human.

cards.title: The Side Door Into a Closed Facility
cards.hook: Journalists can't get inside an immigration detention camp. But when the camp dials 911, the call lands in a county system — where public records law still applies.

cards.title: A Visa Is Permission, Not a Right
cards.hook: A visa does not entitle anyone to stay — it is a revocable permission to ask to be let in. That legal detail is why mass revocations can happen with a signature.

cards.title: When Federal Law Means Different Things in Different States
cards.hook: Nine federal appeals courts have read the same detention statute; seven say one thing and two say the opposite. Until the Supreme Court steps in, your rights depend on your address.

cards.title: Why Moving Children Is a War Crime
cards.hook: International law singles out the transfer of children in wartime for special protection — because taking a child across a border can erase an identity that no ceasefire will restore.

cards.title: When Detention Is a Revenue Line
cards.hook: Contract out a coercive government function and you create a company whose earnings rise with enforcement — and whose shareholders now have a stake in how the policy goes.

cards.title: When Detention Conditions Become a Pressure Tactic
cards.hook: Immigration detention is supposed to hold people while their case is decided — not persuade them to give up on it. Reporting from inside a Texas facility raises exactly that question.

cards.title: Trying Children as Adults
cards.hook: Most legal systems treat young offenders differently — on the logic that a still-developing brain can change. So why are some children still tried in adult courts?

cards.title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
cards.hook: After a world war and the Holocaust, nations did something unprecedented: they wrote down, together, a common list of rights belonging to everyone on Earth.

cards.title: When the Complaint Box Is the Only Oversight
cards.hook: Give people in custody a form to file complaints and you can call it oversight. If nobody outside answers it, the next step isn't another form — it's a hunger strike.

cards.title: Three Kinds of Denial That Let Institutions Off the Hook
cards.hook: Sociologist Stanley Cohen built a typology to explain how societies wave away state atrocities. It turns out to describe how any institution protects its own — one denial at a time.

cards.title: Temporary Protected Status
cards.hook: Some immigrants are allowed to stay not because they won asylum, but because their home country is too dangerous to return to — for now. That 'for now' is the whole idea.

cards.title: Refugees & Asylum
cards.hook: When your own government becomes the threat, your last protection is the right to flee and seek safety elsewhere — the principle at the heart of refugee law.

cards.title: Enforcing Human Rights
cards.hook: Declaring a right is easy; enforcing it against a sovereign state is hard. The global human-rights system relies more on pressure and exposure than on a world police.

cards.title: Three Generations of Rights
cards.hook: Human rights didn't all arrive at once. A useful map sorts them into three 'generations,' each born of a different era's struggles and demanding something different of the state.

cards.title: How You Put a Number on Human Rights
cards.hook: Rights either exist or they don't — so how does anyone score a country? Researchers do it by reading the reports, coding the incidents, and correcting for a nasty bias.

cards.title: The 1789 Law That Let the World Sue in U.S. Courts
cards.hook: One sentence written by the first Congress quietly became America's main door for human rights lawsuits — and the Supreme Court has spent two decades narrowing it.

cards.title: Globalization
cards.hook: The world's economies have woven together so tightly that a decision in one country ripples through all the others — that deepening interdependence is globalization.

cards.title: Global Inequality & Development
cards.hook: Where you're born still shapes your life chances more than almost anything else. Closing that gap between rich and poor nations is one of politics' great unfinished projects.

cards.title: Trade & Protectionism
cards.hook: Should a country trade freely with the world or shield its own industries? This single question has driven economic politics for centuries — and still does.

cards.hook: Governments announce access to vast oil reserves and imply cheaper fuel. Oil in the ground and barrels on the market are separated by years of capital, and by a global price.

cards.title: Why Tariff Fights Escalate
cards.hook: The U.S. put 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods; Canada said within hours it would hit back. That reflex — retaliate, don't absorb — is what turns a tariff into a trade war.

cards.title: What Happens After a Court Voids a Tax
cards.hook: Courts can strike down a tax — but the money is already collected and spent. The unwinding of one tariff program has reached about $100 billion in refunds, and it is far from finished.

cards.title: Tariffs Aimed at Behavior, Not Just Trade
cards.hook: A new round of U.S. tariffs was justified not as shielding domestic industry but as punishing countries for weak enforcement of forced-labor bans — trade policy used as a lever on someone else's laws.

cards.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
cards.hook: When everyone shares a resource but no one owns it, each person's rational choice can add up to collective ruin. That trap explains a huge slice of environmental politics.

cards.title: When a Flood Buyout Can't Reach the People Who Flooded
cards.hook: Disaster buyouts retire dangerous land by purchasing homes. If the residents rent a lot and own a trailer classified as personal property, there is often nothing for the program to buy.

cards.title: Dangerous, But Not Dangerous Enough to Fix
cards.hook: Omaha yards can hold enough lead to harm a child and still fail to qualify for cleanup — because the rule that decides who gets help was written to a 1994 understanding of the risk.

cards.title: Climate Opinion: Party Matters, But Not the Whole Story
cards.hook: Party predicts how Americans feel about climate — but not the whole story: a young Republican may cheer solar panels and still reject a carbon tax.

cards.title: The Great Lakes Program Both Parties Keep Funding
cards.hook: Since 2010 the U.S. has spent over $5 billion cleaning up the Great Lakes — and it has survived Congress after Congress. The coalition behind it is a case study in building bipartisan support.

cards.title: Who Decides Where the Data Center Goes?
cards.hook: A data center brings jobs and tax revenue — and noise, pollution, and higher power bills. Deciding whether to host one is a stress test for local democracy.

cards.title: Precautionary Diplomacy

cards.title: Environmental Governance
cards.hook: How do you regulate something that ignores borders and belongs to no one? Environmental governance is the toolkit societies use to manage nature collectively.

cards.title: The Politics of Climate Change
cards.hook: Climate change is a global commons problem at the largest scale — which is exactly why it's so politically hard: the costs are now, local, and certain; the benefits, future and shared.

cards.title: Protected by a Rule, Not by a Law
cards.hook: Whatever one administration can create with a regulation, the next can undo with a regulation. The move to reopen roadless national forests to logging shows how thin that kind of protection is.

cards.title: Who Checks Whether a Cleanup Held?
cards.hook: The EPA remediated 13,000 Omaha yards and moved on. Reporters retested 620 of them for $10 a sample — and found lead above the agency's own trigger in four of every ten.

cards.title: Rulemaking Is Supposed to Include the Public — What Happens When It Doesn't
cards.hook: Before a federal agency can change a regulation, it's normally required to ask the public first. A 2026 overhaul of grazing rules on federal land tested how easily that step can be trimmed.

cards.title: How Redefining One Word Can Rewrite a Law
cards.hook: Congress didn't touch the Endangered Species Act. An agency just redefined what "habitat" means — and, critics say, quietly stripped out one of its main protections.

cards.title: Can Carbon Capture Solve Climate Change?
cards.hook: What if we could keep burning fossil fuels and just vacuum the carbon back out? That promise is seductive, politically powerful — and, a major investigation argues, a mirage.

cards.title: War & Peace
cards.hook: War is politics at its most extreme — organized violence between groups. Understanding why it happens, and how peace is kept, is central to the study of states.

cards.title: The Office Whose Job Is Counting the Wrong Deaths
cards.hook: Militaries do not automatically learn from killing civilians. Somebody has to be paid to investigate it, and that office can be closed as easily as it was opened.

cards.title: Sanctions: The Weapon States Reach For Before They Reach For Weapons
cards.hook: Cutting a country off from money and markets sits between a strongly-worded letter and a war — which is exactly why governments use it so often, and why it so often disappoints.

cards.title: When a Temporary Deployment Stops Being Temporary
cards.hook: Emergency powers rarely end with an announcement. They end — or don't — through quiet extensions that never get the scrutiny the first decision did.

cards.title: Why Moving Children Is a War Crime
cards.hook: International law singles out the transfer of children in wartime for special protection — because taking a child across a border can erase an identity that no ceasefire will restore.

cards.title: The 60-Day Clock That Keeps Getting Reset
cards.hook: The War Powers Resolution gives Congress 60 days to approve a war before the president must stop — but a new 'notice' can restart the clock, and Congress has struggled to make its objection stick.

cards.title: Giving a Country Weapons vs. Teaching It to Build Them

cards.title: Terrorism Charges Without an Ideology
cards.hook: Texas is prosecuting a teenage shooting spree as terrorism with no manifesto and no extremist ties — testing whether the crime is defined by motive or by the fear it creates.

cards.title: Why Ceasefires Break Down
cards.hook: A ceasefire stops the shooting. It does not make peace. The difference — and the danger — lies in everything a quick deal leaves out.

cards.title: The Director of National Intelligence
cards.hook: After 9/11, the U.S. created one job to make its spy agencies talk to each other — and a veteran argues the role needs expertise, not just political loyalty.

cards.title: Terrorism
cards.hook: Terrorism is violence aimed less at its victims than at an audience — using fear as a political weapon to force change a group cannot win by other means.

cards.title: Nuclear Weapons & Deterrence
cards.hook: How do you stop a war you could never survive? The nuclear age answered with a chilling paradox: build weapons so terrible that no one dares use them.

cards.title: A Voting Rule Needs a System Behind It
cards.hook: Writing a new election rule is the easy part. Building the machinery that can execute it before the next election is where rules quietly turn into disenfranchisement.

cards.title: Scientific Integrity Policies Are Only Words Until Tested
cards.hook: Agencies that produce official numbers usually have a written rule barring political interference. It is an internal policy — which means the same agency can edit it.

cards.title: The Deepfake That Doesn't Have to Fool You Twice
cards.hook: The most effective synthetic video isn't the most realistic one. It's the one that looks like something you already scroll past every day — a talk-show clip about yesterday's news.

cards.title: When Officials Sign an NDA
cards.hook: A nondisclosure agreement is a private contract. When public officials sign one, the public loses its normal claim on what its own government is negotiating.

cards.title: Can AI Verify a Signature on a Ballot? Experts Say Not Yet
cards.hook: The FBI explored using AI to check signatures on seized mail-in ballots — a case study in what happens when new technology meets an old, imperfect forensic method.

cards.title: FISA Section 702
cards.hook: The law behind much of America's foreign-intelligence collection — powerful enough to feed most of the president's daily brief, yet it expires unless Congress keeps renewing it.

cards.title: Surveillance & Privacy
cards.hook: Technology lets states and companies watch people at a scale once unimaginable — putting the old right to be left alone on a collision course with security and profit.

cards.title: Technology & Democracy
cards.hook: The internet promised to supercharge democracy — more voice, more information, more connection. It delivered that, and a tangle of new threats alongside it.

cards.title: A Strict Privacy Law Is Only as Strong as Its Enforcer
cards.hook: A state can write the toughest data privacy law in the country and still see the data sold. Rights on paper need someone whose job is to notice when they're ignored.

cards.title: When the Constitution Says Nothing Yet
cards.hook: About 96,000 American children were born through IVF in 2023. The Supreme Court has barely addressed the technology — leaving state courts to invent the rules one dispute at a time.

cards.title: When a 'Candidate' Texting You Is Actually a Bot
cards.hook: Campaigns have always texted voters. Now some of those texts are AI-generated conversations trained to sound like the candidate — personalized, responsive, and not always clearly labeled.

cards.title: A Law Can Take Effect Before Courts Decide If It's Legal
cards.hook: Texas requires parental permission before minors can download most apps. Courts haven't ruled it constitutional — but the Supreme Court's emergency docket let it take effect anyway.

cards.title: States Are Writing AI Law First — and Federal Preemption Looms Over All of It
cards.hook: With no comprehensive federal AI law yet, states have become the testing ground for regulating artificial intelligence. That leaves every state AI law exposed to a preemption fight.

cards.title: Who Decides Where the Data Center Goes?
cards.hook: A data center brings jobs and tax revenue — and noise, pollution, and higher power bills. Deciding whether to host one is a stress test for local democracy.

cards.title: Prediction Markets in Politics
cards.hook: Let people bet real money on who wins, and the prices start to look like odds — a crowd-sourced forecast. But betting on politics invites its own kind of trouble.

cards.title: Why Census Data Has 'Noise' Added
cards.hook: To stop anyone reverse-engineering your identity from public statistics, the U.S. census deliberately blurs its own numbers — a privacy-for-accuracy trade with real political stakes.

cards.title: Gunshot Detection Tech
cards.hook: Cities pay millions for microphones that promise to pinpoint gunfire and speed up police. The evidence that it actually works is surprisingly thin.

cards.title: When 'AI Safety' Becomes Leverage
cards.hook: Rules meant to protect the public can be turned into tools of control. One scholar argues some governments are repurposing 'AI safety' to pressure tech companies into line.

cards.title: When Speed of Access to Official Speech Is for Sale
cards.hook: A leader's posts move markets and policy. What happens to equal access when a company charges customers to receive them milliseconds sooner?

cards.title: Who Gets to Regulate Betting on Elections?
cards.hook: Wisconsin says you can't bet on an election you vote in — a law from 1849. The biggest prediction market calls that 'voter suppression.' Underneath sits a bigger question: which government decides?

cards.title: Geofence Warrants & the Fourth Amendment
cards.hook: Police can ask a tech company which phones were near a crime scene at a given hour — sweeping up everyone's location, not just a suspect's. In 2026 the Court said that's a 'search.'

cards.title: When a Governor Pauses an Entire Industry by Executive Order
cards.hook: Data-center fights used to be decided lot by lot, in local zoning meetings. In 2026 a governor skipped that entirely and paused the whole industry statewide.
